result:
I have always suspected that the moon keeps a small library behind its craters. Not books, exactly, but memories folded into silver rectangles, each one glowing with the intentions of someone who looked upward on a lonely night. On clear evenings, the librarian—a quiet owl with ink-stained wings—sorts them by longing.

One morning, I found an envelope on my kitchen table. It contained a photograph of a train I had never seen and a note in my own handwriting: “Take the 8:15 tomorrow. You will understand.” Naturally, I ignored this advice, because following instructions written in your own hand is the sort of thing that leads either to enlightenment or an unexpectedly long conversation with railway staff.

Instead, I spent the day rearranging chairs, watering a fern, and arguing with the refrigerator. The refrigerator hummed a low B-flat and refused to explain itself. At sunset, the train appeared anyway, floating silently above the rooftops. Its windows were filled with golden light, and every passenger seemed to be holding a small, unfinished story.

I climbed aboard. The conductor asked where I wanted to go, so I said, “Somewhere I have not been disappointed yet.” She smiled and rang the bell.

Even now, I cannot say whether that journey changed my life. Perhaps it simply gave me a better question to carry home.

Tomorrow, I may board a strange vehicle, or return to the moon’s library to submit a memory. Either way, I hope the librarian saves me a fascinating story.
